newsitem.title: FRANCE: French employers to fete 50 years of influence.
newsitem.headline: French employers to fete 50 years of influence.

text.p: The French employers' federation, long a key social partner to the state and labour unions, will mark its 50th jubilee on Monday with a paean to entrepreneurs and a reassertion of its relevance to the French economy.

In the historic city of Poitiers, the Conseil Nationale du Patronat Francais (CNPF), will celebrate a half-century of prominence with a day of festivities capped by an address from President Jacques Chirac at 1500 GMT.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis will also attend, as will a host of CNPF officials including its president Jean Gandois, former head of aluminium group Pechiney.

The event, which CNPF officials have pledged to keep free of references to disputes with the government, is likely to paper over sometimes deep differences over how to help fix France's stubborn economic woes.
Founded in the aftermath of World War Two, the Patronat as it is familiarly known, was among the central pillars supporting and directing the economy.
But its role has weakened over the years as new forces came to bear in France's gradually deregulated economy.

While it still negotiates with labour unions and the government over wages and industrial matters, it has increasingly been cast in the role of free-market booster in opposition to state and labour, which have been slower to change and have sought to retain more control over the economy.
"We believe in competition, we believe in the marketplace, we are for companies with a lot of capital and strong profitability," said Denis Kessler, a CNPF vice president.
"We must also be extremely solid partners in front of public powers, in front of the unions," Kessler said in a radio interview on Saturday.

The CNPF backs many of the government's positions, including stout support for France's entry into a single European currency, but has a record of vocal opposition to government efforts to micromanage the economy.

"In the interdependent and unpredictable world we live in today, the state has to understand that the answers will come from further down, not on high, and that its role is not to manage and regulate everything, but to encourage initiative and above all foster confidence in the assets which create wealth and employment," CNPF vice president Pierre Ballon said in May.

Gandois, whose election in November 1994 thwarted a rival bid from a building magnate close to Chirac, has had several prickly exchanges with the President, highlighting the CNPF's willingness to stand up to the government to defend its members.
After Chirac criticised companies last January for not hiring more in return for tax cuts, Gandois told the President he could not force corporations to act against their interests.
"I am getting sick and tired of hearing talk of presents being handed out to companies and the efforts company bosses should be making when many of them are fighting to survive," Gandois added.
The celebration on Monday is likely to focus more on charting a future for the CNPF, whose membership recognises the need for change, Kessler said.

"I think (the CNPF) must adapt to its environment exactly as all other organisations and institutions," he said. "We are aware of this and for a year and a half now we have been looking at what role there is for an employers' federation in 1996."
